Tutor Perini Stock Rises 20% in the Past 3 Months: Time to Buy Yet?

J

Tutor Perini Corporation TPC has climbed 19.7% over the past three months, outperforming the Zacks Building Products - Heavy Construction industry, the broader Zacks Construction sector and the S&P 500 Index.

The multi-year public infrastructure spending trends are creating growth opportunities for the company, especially across civil infrastructure, buildings and specialty contracting projects. With these market tailwinds, TPC has the leverage to ensure shareholder value and demonstrate efforts toward meaningful margin improvement.

Even though project delays and execution risks loom over the company, as it is associated with government-related and large-scale projects, the market tailwinds are supporting Tutor Perini's growth prospects.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Let us decode the positive and negative factors that are shaping TPC stock's prospects.

What is Boosting Tutor Perini's Growth Momentum?

Strong Backlog & Infrastructure Demand: Tutor Perini's near-record $19.9 billion backlog provides substantial revenue visibility and positions it to benefit from sustained infrastructure spending. Demand remains strong across civil infrastructure, buildings and specialty contracting, supported by well-funded federal, state and local customers. The company is also benefiting from large-scale projects tied to grid modernization, transportation, defense infrastructure and data centers. Its pipeline has expanded to more than $200 billion, offering significant opportunities for future backlog replenishment. The nine mega-projects secured in recent years, worth approximately $16 billion collectively, should support growth as execution ramps up. Management's selective bidding strategy, combined with favorable project opportunities in the Indo-Pacific, California, Midwest and Northeast, further strengthens the long-term growth outlook.

Margin Expansion Efforts: TPC is demonstrating meaningful margin improvement as higher-margin mega-projects ramp up and execution strengthens. The Civil segment generated a 15.3% operating margin in the second quarter of 2026, above the company's 12-15% target range, while Building margins improved to 5.6%, near the upper end of its 3-6% target. Most notably, the Specialty Contractors segment recovered to a 2.2% margin from a negative 10.2% margin a year ago, reflecting improving execution in New York and Texas electrical and mechanical projects. Management expects these projects to ramp over several years and is targeting a sustainable 5-8% Specialty margin over time. Lower corporate expenses, reduced interest costs and potential contingency releases from mega-projects could provide additional earnings leverage.

Capital Allocation & Shareholder Returns: Tutor Perini's significantly stronger balance sheet is enhancing financial flexibility while creating opportunities to return capital to shareholders. At the end of June 2026, cash exceeded total debt by approximately $542 million, while cash available for general corporate purposes reached $424 million. The company is deploying this liquidity through share repurchases, dividends, strategic investments and support for its bonding requirements. During the second quarter of 2026, TPC repurchased approximately 137,000 shares for $10 million and raised its quarterly dividend by 50% to nine cents. Lower financing costs and disciplined capital allocation should support earnings and shareholder value.

Raised 2026 Outlook: Tutor Perini's raised 2026 outlook reinforces confidence in its improving earnings trajectory. The company increased its adjusted EPS guidance to $5.15-$5.45, from $4.90-$5.30, following stronger-than-expected first-half execution. The revised outlook reflects growing contributions from newer, higher-margin mega-projects, improved operating margins across all three segments and expectations for continued strong cash generation. Management also expects 2027 adjusted EPS to be substantially above the upper end of the revised 2026 range, supported by the nearly $20 billion backlog and increasing project activity. Importantly, the 2026 guidance still incorporates significant contingency for unexpected developments, providing some cushion against execution risks.

Major U.S. stock indices ended Sept. 9, 2026, on a dismal note as rising oil prices and inflation worries kept the bourses under pressure for the third consecutive day. Meanwhile, bond yields climbed higher, with the 10-year yield hitting 4.836%, further hurting investor optimism in the stock market.

Amid this backdrop, investors must be increasingly forced to recalibrate their equity risk as macro headwinds converge on multiple fronts. Notably, a sharp resurgence in energy costs—driven by Middle East supply disruptions that pushed Brent crude past $100 a barrel—has amplified anxieties over persistent consumer and wholesale inflation. 

With money markets now pricing in a heightened probability of further Federal Reserve rate hikes to combat sticky input costs, investors might want to pivot toward financially resilient, low-leverage stocks. 

Backed by strong balance sheets, high coverage ratios, and robust free cash flow, low-leverage stocks emerge as a prudent defensive strategy to survive an increasingly restrictive monetary and economic environment. 

To this end, we recommend low-leverage stocks, such as LifeStance Health Group LFST, Tutor Perini TPC, News Corporation NWS, Everus Construction Group ECG and HF Sinclair DINO. Before selecting low-leverage stocks, it is important to understand what leverage is and how investing in low-leverage companies can benefit investors.

What's the Significance of Low-Leverage Stocks?

In finance, leverage refers to the use of borrowed capital to support business operations and drive expansion. Companies typically raise such funds through debt financing, although equity financing remains an alternative. However, firms often prefer debt due to its relatively lower cost and easier availability compared to issuing equity.

Debt financing comes with inherent risks and is beneficial only when it generates returns that exceed the cost of borrowing. To limit downside risk, investors should be cautious of companies that rely excessively on debt. Prudent investing involves selecting businesses with manageable leverage, as completely debt-free companies are rare.

The equity market can be volatile at times. As an investor, if you want to avoid significant losses, we suggest focusing on stocks with low leverage, which are generally deemed less risky.

To identify such stocks, several leverage ratios have historically been developed to measure the amount of debt a company carries. The debt-to-equity ratio is among the most widely used financial ratios.

Read almost any review of the new $1,999 iPhone Duo (that's the base price). It's just as good as, if not better than, the mini iPad, reviewers say. That opens the question of whether people will buy the Duo at the higher price.

The Duo will likely be bundled with three-year subscriptions from AT&T (NYSE: T), Verizon (NYSE: VZ), and T-Mobile. Verizon charges $33.33 for the iPhone 17 Pro Max. But that includes a three-year subscription to Verizon's cellular network. The Duo will be sold the same way. The monthly price will probably be closer to $60, given the Duo's retail price. Spread over 36 months, the deal may be a bargain for those desperate to own one.

Kyu3a / Wikimedia Commons

The Duo has a 7.6-inch screen when open. The iPad mini is 8.3 inches measured as a rectangle. Cellular models with high storage capacity can push the mini's price as high as $899. That means the Duo is more than twice as expensive.

Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), of course, is selling the Duo as a product light-years ahead of anything else it has launched. "The largest iPhone display ever. Foldable, posable, standable. Featuring unique iOS experiences for ultimate versatility," Apple said. Apple released the first iPad mini in 2012. Although it has been updated since then, in "Apple years" it is really old.

Wells Fargo's Steven Cahall used a CNBC segment on September 8 to reframe SpaceX's (NASDAQ:SPCX) wireless push. He argues that satellite-plus-spectrum architecture needs less ground infrastructure than a traditional fourth carrier, so the pain falls on incumbent telcos while tower REITs and cable operators quietly collect rent on whatever pieces SpaceX still has to lease.

jurvetson / Flickr

Cahall told CNBC: "Telco just facing another competitor, a three player market going to a much smaller fourth player. That's still a net negative for sure."

The FCC just cleared SpaceX to absorb 65 MHz of EchoStar's U.S. spectrum, and Starlink subscribers doubled year over year to 12.0 million as of Q2 2026. That makes the question urgent for anyone holding AT&T (NYSE:T), Verizon (NYSE:VZ), T-Mobile (NASDAQ:TMUS), American Tower (NYSE:AMT), Crown Castle (NYSE:CCI), SBA Communications (NASDAQ:SBAC), Charter Communications (NASDAQ:CHTR) or Comcast (NASDAQ:CMCSA).

What Cahall Said About the Fourth-Carrier Debate

Cahall broke from the standard fourth-carrier framing. He said, "We don't think it's because the economics of adding a fourth player to the U.S. wireless market is so compelling. It's that there are ulterior long term technology motives."
